newsitem.title: USA: AMR could lose market share in strike.
newsitem.headline: AMR could lose market share in strike.

text.p: American Airlines could permanently lose market share in Chicago and other key cities if pilots strike the airline this weekend.
Most major U.S. airlines said they will offer their empty seats to AMR Corp's American's passengers if last-ditch talks between the airline and its pilots fail before the weekend deadline.
American would be particularly vulnerable to a strike at this time as many of its flights carry passengers to the warmer Caribbean vacation destinations from the mainland U.S.

The pilots could strike on February 15 -- disrupting travel plans during the hectic President's Day holiday weekend, one of the industry's busiest periods during the typically slower winter travel season.
While a strike would hurt the entire U.S. airline industry due to mounting labor woes, UAL Corp's United Airlines and Continental Airlines Inc could see substantial benefits, analysts said.
United and American have competing hubs at Chicago's O'Hare airport and United could quickly grab a larger share of that market, analysts said.

"American would have a tough time getting that market back," said Brian Harris, an airline analyst at Lehman Brothers. American's absence during a strike would also give United an edge on profitable transcontinental routes, Harris said.
United, however, said it is limited in the number of planes and seats it can offer to American's passengers immediately after the strike deadline.

"Our fleet is fully deployed. It's a get-away weekend for many people, so we are limited in what we can do as far as adding to the fleet," said Joe Hopkins, a spokesman for UAL Corp's United Airlines.
Continental Airlines Inc could stake claim to some of American's Latin American market share through aggressive marketing and service improvements out of its Newark hub, analysts said.
Continental said it plans to add flights to key markets and increase staffing if a strike occurs. The airlines declined to provide additional details.
Trans World Airlines Inc also said it may add flights in Chicago, Dallas and San Juan.
Delta Air Lines Inc, which reduced service in Dallas in December 1995, menawhile could use the strike as a chance to rebuild its presence there.
But Delta's benefit would be slim, since American would easily regain dominance in its home town, analysts said.
USAir Group Inc and other major airlines said they are willing to provide assistance to American passengers, but the are limited in the number of seats they can provide.
American has "interline" agreements with all the major carriers, expect Southwest Airlines Co. The agreements allow carriers to accept a competitor's tickets if they have seats available.

Airlines said Tuesday they were developing guidelines on which American tickets would be accepted. Some tickets bought with frequent-flyer points or at huge discounts may not be accepted at all airlines. Southwest said it was in talks with American about accepting some passengers.
